Lihikenstein joined the United Nations
36 years ago as its60th

We did so driven by the conviction that
we as one of the smallest members of the
international community should be part
of the most important conversation on
global governance with the participation
of all states big or small in developing
international norms and standards and
also in upholding respect for them.
Sovereignty was a key theme of our
domestic discussions resulting in our UN
membership.
We joined out of enlightened
self-interest, the belief that we need
the UN to secure respect for our
sovereignty through upholding
international law as the basis for our

To this end, we also decided to make our
own contribution to make best use of the

President,
our belief in the United Nations remains
steadfast.
This is the place where we can make our
voice heard, where we can put ideas
forward and where we can gather to try
to solve the issues that affect us all.
We have greatly benefited from our
membership and the UN has consistently
been a key platform for our foreign
policy.
Our membership has consistently enjoyed
high levels of support in our
population.
But today we also find ourselves in a
moment where instability and uncertainty
dominate the conversation.
Our organization no longer seems able to
deliver on the key promise of the UN
charter to save future generations from
the scourge of war.
It can no longer count on the
unconditional support of its most
powerful members for the guiding rules
of international law.
It is increasingly ignored or sidelined
in a efforts to address both the
traditional and new challenges such as
the regulation of artificial
intelligence.
It is permanently squeezed financially.
legal obligations to pay are turned into
tools to exercise political leverage.
As a result, the United Nations has
moved down the foreign policy agenda,
even of states who have a strong history
of supporting it.
We can no longer take it for granted
that our people will continue their
strongly positive views of our
organization.
President, this is the difficult moment
in which we find ourselves.
But rather than engaging in doomsday
scenarios, we have to find the
opportunities hidden in the challenge.
The overwhelming majority of the states
present in this room believe in the
United Nations. They want to see
positive change for the UN to emerge
stronger, more effective, more relevant.
But we all have to be prepared to be
part of the change that we want to see.
Resisting the temptation of collective
inertia and of waiting for positive
change to happen on its own will require
our active political investment.
We're grateful to Secretary General
Guterish for his service to the
organization and for his proposals to
adapt the organization to the needs of
today.
On the basis of his ideas, our
delegations here have done good work
that will show positive results over
time. This is important.
It shows that we can come together also
during times of deep political division.
It is also not enough.
The steps we have taken are just the
beginning of what we need. A political
agreement that combines significant
structural change with a reliable
financial commitment and firm support
for the UN charter from all.
This is also the vision we are looking
for in the person that will be appointed
as the next secretary general.
We hope that this decision will come

prepare for these most unique of jobs.
And we remain convinced that having a
woman at the helm of the United Nations
is long overdue
for an organization that prides itself
on its role in gender equality.

At its core, the United Nations is a
peace organization.
This is the promise of the UN charter
and this is what our people expect from
the UN and the reason why they hold it
in high esteem.
Over the past year, we have seen a
record number of armed conflicts around
the world and a rapidly diminishing role
of the United Nations in ending them.
In the Middle East, the UN's role has
been further reduced in contrast to the
central position it has taken up over
the years. In Ukraine, there are few
prospects for a peace process, even
though the aggression has now lasted
longer than World War I without even a
nominal role for the United Nations. In
Sudan, the role of the UN is limited to
alleviating the enormous suffering of
the civilian population with no prospect
of a political solution and the end to
the conflict.
We are well aware of the political
dynamic in the security council
primarily tasked with matters of peace
and security which severely limits the
options for UN action. But the
conversation must not end there. There
are alternatives for action. This
assembly in particular has wide
authority over over matters of peace and
security and it is universal in
composition.
A glance at its history demonstrates its
authority in peacekeeping,
conflict termination and accountability.
It is time that we make better use of
this authority.
The veto initiative which we were proud
to spearhead provides a platform for
such action. What is required is the
will to spend our political capital here
in this room on peace rather than force
by dealing with conflict through
diplomacy rather than through war.
The United Nations must not accept being
reduced to a crisis mitigation
organization
that distributes states contributions to
a skyrocketing humanitarian assistance
bill. Instead, we need to see a return
to the UN doing political work to
prevent, contain, and end conflict
through the wide range of peace
operations available and through a
strong interplay between a secretary
general who is proactive and offers
creative solutions backed by the UN
membership.
President, any successful community must
be grounded in the rule of law and so it
is with the international community.
Our commitment to the law as the
foundation for the conduct of
international affairs is grounded both
in principle and pragmatism.
The biggest strength of the United
Nations is that it is firmly grounded in
rules we have all agreed on and that we
have all agreed apply to all of us.
This foundational agreement is
increasingly challenged with alarming
trends to dismiss and ignore
international law altogether which can
only result in a world where might makes
right.
This would result in catastrophic human
cost, a further proliferation of
conflict, and have devastating effects
on development and on human security.
We hope that both small and medium-sized
states will come together in our common
interest for a strong multilateral
system on the basis of respect for
international law.
This is the moment for us to unify in
support of what the United Nations is
built on.
President, naturally, we are also strong
supporters of international courts, the
indispensable enforcement mechanisms of
international law. Likenstein joined the
jurisdiction of the international court
of justice four decades before we joined
the UN. You have made more submissions
to the court over the past decade than
in its entire history before. We
strongly support its work and its
competence in both its advisory and
dispute settlement functions. We
encourage all to join us in submitting
to the compulsory jurisdiction of the
court.
Likenstein is also strongly committed to
the International Criminal Court, the
first permanent international court with
jurisdiction over the most serious
crimes under international law,
genocide, crimes against humanity, war
crimes, and the crime of aggression. We
will continue to support the court and
its mandate to ensure accountability and
its central message that nobody is above
the law.
In joining the ICC, we have exercised
our sovereignty and delegated the
jurisdiction we have ourselves to an
international court which we have helped
create. We are proud of the way the
court has addressed the challenges to
its resilience over the past year in the
face of re relentless political attacks
and unpre unprecedented sanctions.
We hope that more states will join this
project which is one of the landmark
achievements in the history of
international treatym.
The Rome statute also criminalizes the
supreme international crime, the crime
of aggression which complements the
prohibition of the illegal use of force,
the core piece of the UN charter. At the
international level, by signing the UN
charter, we have all agreed to refrain
from the threat of or use of force
against the territorial integrity or
political independence of another state.
This is the most ambitious collective
commitment to end war that has ever
existed. Amidst accelerating human
suffering the world over, it has never
been more important for us to implement
this commitment.
President, it has now been many decades
since scientists first warned us of the
dangers of climate change. Nevertheless,
we have continued to run into the
climate abbies, leaving the coming chaos
for our children and their children. It
is almost impossible to believe that we
need to reiterate the facts. The climate
crisis is real.
We are seeing its effects every day.
From heat waves that bake the soil to
heavy rains that turned the parched
ground into mud. People are starving in
the heat and drowning in the floods.
Crops can no longer be sustainably
harvested. Animals and pollinators are
dying out. Likenstein commits to working
with all states to address these harms
and to reverse these trends as much as
we still can.
We support the advisory opinion of the
International Court of Justice on
climate change and this week we were
proud to join the adoption of a high
level declaration on sea level rise
including a commitment to the continuity
of statethood for all UN member states.
Only a few years ago member states in
this debate wondered aloud if their name
plates would be switched off. The
commitment we made this week is to
guarantee that this will not happen in
the face of seas which inundate whole
territories. Standing up for
self-determination is the least we can
do for those most affected.
President,
this week has also seen an intense
debate on harnessing the potential of
artificial intelligence.
But perhaps what we are discovering in
these conversations are our own limits
to understanding what the that potential
might be.
Reporting from the most powerful and
well- capitalized AI companies tell us
that we are on a precipice either of a
technologyfueled
utopia or an apocalypse.
Whether we achieve one or the other
unfortunately has been treated as a
secondary priority to the AI race, one
that has no clear finish line and for
that matter a dubious price.
Likenstein supports the regulation of
artificial intelligence.
Unless we have a clear understanding of
the methods, processes and purposes of
the huge variety of AI systems, how can
we risk the consequences to human
rights, to our environment, to the
long-term capacities for our critical
thinking, and ultimately to the future
of the human species.
We are already seeing the impacts on
civilians as armed forces increasingly
integrate AI capabilities into their
targeting systems in warfare.
AI tools have to be made for humanity
lest we become the source material for
AI systems to use or merely the victims
in its crosshairs.
